sections.html:
Richmond is an independent city, so one government values, bills and collects. The Office of the Assessor of Real Estate sets values. The Department of Finance sends the bills and takes the money.

  • Assessor of Real Estate: (804) 646-7500, assessmentappeals@rva.gov, City Hall, 900 E. Broad St., Room 802. Open Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.
  • Department of Finance, Real Estate Unit: (804) 646-7000 or RVA311.com, 900 E. Broad St.

Finance asks residents to send questions through the city's RVA 311 system. Real estate tax is levied on each $100 of assessed value and collected in two billings a year.

The first half of the real estate tax is due January 14, and the second half is due June 14. January 1 is the date the value of real estate is established. Reassessment notices go out on or about July 1 each year with a value date of July 1, so read your notice for the exact date it uses.

DateWhat is due or set
January 1Value of real estate established
January 14Real estate tax, first half
January 20 and April 20Short-term rental property taxes, fourth and first quarter
June 5Personal property tax for vehicles, boats, trailers and motorcycles
June 14Real estate tax, second half

The city also has an online request form for a penalty and interest waiver, found through RVA 311. Finance can tell you what applies to your account. If you rent your house short term, settle the quarterly rental tax before you list so no old balance surprises the closing agent, and ask Finance how those taxes are handled at a sale.

Richmond lists three steps: an office review, then the Board of Equalization, then a direct appeal to the court.

Each owner's last known address receives a notice on or about July 1 listing the proposed assessment, earlier values and the calculated change in tax. Before you ask for a formal review, call the assessor's front desk at (804) 646-7500 and talk with the area appraiser. The assessor's page has a tool for finding your residential neighborhood.

  • Bring recent comparable sales close to the assessment date.
  • Check the recorded square footage, bedroom count and condition notes.
  • Expect an uphill case: Va. Code 58.1-3379 presumes the assessor's value is correct and puts the burden on the taxpayer.

The city can auction property whose real estate tax has gone unpaid for a long time. The program was paused in January 2023 and is returning, with the first sale expected in the second half of 2027.

Va. Code 58.1-3965 makes a property eligible after two full calendar years of delinquent tax, or after one year when it is condemned, a nuisance, derelict or blighted.

  • Eligibility: the City Attorney reviews delinquent accounts.
  • Notice: owners and occupants are mailed a Notice of Intent.
  • Options: set up a payment plan, or redeem by paying taxes, penalties, interest and legal fees.
  • Auction: an account still unpaid goes to a Special Commissioner, who sells at public auction.

Unbuildable properties and properties whose owners are in bankruptcy are not eligible. A payment arrangement can stop a sale as long as it stays in good standing. The city limits owners to one tax type at a time and one new arrangement per 12 months.

Finance runs the Older Adults and Persons with Disabilities Real Estate Tax Relief Program, and the Assessor runs an exemption for disabled ex-service members. Each has its own application. Applications and recertifications come with deadlines, so call Finance for the current date before you plan around it.

Real estate tax ranks first among liens in Virginia, which means any balance is deducted from your sale proceeds.

Va. Code 58.1-3340 has the buyer or a foreclosure trustee send proceeds to the tax first, penalties and interest too. How the year is shared between you and the buyer is a contract matter. A grantor's tax of 50 cents per $500 of value is added to the deed under Va. Code 58.1-802, and the seller usually pays it. Deeds for the city are recorded by Richmond's Circuit Court clerk.

  • Call Finance through RVA 311 for a payoff before you accept a closing date.
  • Ask whether the city has put the property into the tax sale program, since Finance takes no further collection action on accounts in that program.
  • Ask the closing agent to confirm that the lien release is recorded.

Owners with back taxes, tenants or a house that needs repairs often compare a direct sale with listing. In both cases the tax payoff comes out of the proceeds.

Richmond is the capital of Virginia, set at the fall line of the James River, with 226,610 residents at the 2020 census. Because it has no county layer, the same city government handles every part of the tax. Neighborhoods vary widely, from Shockoe Bottom and Carytown to the Fan District, Oregon Hill and the East End, which includes Church Hill, Fulton, Union Hill and Fairmount. Values and tax histories differ from one to the next, so use comparable sales from your own neighborhood.

sections.h2: What to have ready when you call
sections.html:
Have the property address, the account number from your bill and the name on the deed in front of you. For an assessment question, add the notice you received and any photos or repair estimates that show why the value is off. When you use RVA 311, note the reference number so a later call to Finance can pick up where the first one stopped. If the owner has died or you are acting for a relative, ask which documents Finance wants to see before it will talk about the account. These small steps save a second trip downtown. They matter more once a closing date is set, because a missing document can push the payoff past the day you planned to sign.

If you plan to appeal and sell in the same year, tell the title company and your agent. A pending review can change the tax figure on the settlement statement, and the contract should say who benefits if the value comes down.

Ask Finance for a payoff through RVA 311 and write down the date you called. Check that the account is not in the tax sale program, because Finance stops collecting on accounts that are. Compare the payoff with the amount on your most recent bill, and ask about any difference you cannot explain. Confirm which half-year payment is already made. Read the contract's proration clause. Then ask the closing agent to record the lien release and send you a copy. If you applied for tax relief, tell Finance about the sale so the file is updated, and ask whether any credit applies for the part of the year you owned the house.

faqs.q: When are Richmond real estate taxes due?
faqs.a: The first half is due January 14 and the second half June 14.

faqs.q: Who do I call about a Richmond assessment?
faqs.a: The Assessor of Real Estate at (804) 646-7500 or assessmentappeals@rva.gov. Billing questions go through RVA 311 at (804) 646-7000.

faqs.q: When does Richmond send reassessment notices?
faqs.a: On or about July 1 each year, with a value date of July 1.

faqs.q: Can Richmond sell my house for unpaid taxes?
faqs.a: Yes, through its tax sale program, once taxes are delinquent for two full calendar years, or one year for condemned, derelict or blighted property.

faqs.q: Can I stop a Richmond tax sale?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Owners can redeem by paying taxes, penalties, interest and legal fees before the auction, or enter a payment plan. Call 311 to ask about your account.
